subsubtopic: REQUEST FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE BE PROVIDED TO ROCKWELL INTERNATIONAL PLANTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of extreme urgency particularly in so far as the employees of Rockwell International, one of the plants in my riding, are concerned.
This plant is involved in the production of wheel discs and other auto parts for many of the large automobile companies. Since 1978, the number of employees at this plant in Parry Sound has been significantly reduced, from 220 employees in 1978 to 75 at present. On June 6 of this year, the plant will officially close. The Rockwell International plant at Brace-bridge has also experienced severe financial setbacks in recent years, although I understand they will continue to operate. The plant at Parry Sound has on more than one occasion been outbid by a Rockwell International plant in Mississippi, a sister plant.
In view of the fact that this government has seen fit to give Chrysler Canada a $200 million aid package in an attempt to salvage the company, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the government undertake a firm commitment forthwith to provide similar financial assistance to the Rockwell International plants in Parry Sound and Braccbridge, in an attempt to assist these plants to survive the profound financial difficulties that they are presently facing as a result of their having to compete with plants in the southern United States where the cost of labour is considerably less expensive.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR COMMITTEE REVIEW OF GUN LAWS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provision of Standing Order 43, to present an urgent and pressing matter.
Whereas the Magna Carta ensures that no man shall be dispossessed of his rights without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land; and whereas, under Canada's gun laws, an officer does not have to secure a search warrant for a search of a person's home but only has to believe there is just cause for the search; and whereas an officer may search a person's home and, under the provisions of the gun laws, may seize all firearms held by him without even laying a charge; and whereas there are a number of other inequities and inequalities contrary to British justice in our gun control laws, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That the gun laws be referred for review and amendment to the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee at the earliest possible time.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my motion is one I believe will receive the support of the whole House. I believe it deals with the objectives of all members of this chamber in seeing a more fulfilling role for women in our society, and particularly that this Parliament should lead in that way. It is in respect of our rule book of the House of

May 23, 1980

Commons Chamber which makes reference to members of Parliament and to Madam Speaker as "Mr. Speaker", which leads to so many of the, "Mr.-I mean, Madam Speaker" that we hear. I note on page 7 of the Standing Orders, as one example, the following:
When a member is speaking, no member shall pass between him and the Chair, nor interrupt him-
That is as if members of Parliament are male. Also on page 23, Standing Order 28 reads as follows:
Every member desiring to speak is to rise in his place ... and address himself to Mr. Speaker.
Virtually every page makes reference to members or the Speaker as being male. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean):
That in the next printing of the Standing Orders of the House of Commons, which we encourage to be soon, the male gender in reference to members of Parliament and the Speaker be removed and replaced by articles of neutral gender so that reference may be made to either or both sexes.

OIL IMPORT POLICY OF GOVERNMENT-IMPORT COMPENSATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister yesterday confirmed in this House that his government will phase out the oil compensation subsidy, and that the Canadian price for crude oil will be a blend of imported and domestic crude prices. This means the federal government will no longer contribute the estimated $3.1 billion or more for this year to cushion the impact on the consumer of higher imported costs.
My question is: where will that money come from? Will it be picked up directly by the consumers through high crude oil prices? Will there be some special tax or levy operating outside the Consolidated Revenue Fund, or will the producing provinces be requested to pick up this $3.1 billion?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Solicitor General. In view of the Officials Secrets Act charges that were pursued against Peter Treu, pursued against Peter Worthington, editor of The Toronto Sun, and almost pursued against myself as a member of this House, will the minister give the House all the reasons why the government has closed the case against Professor Hambleton, of Montreal, who confessed to a representative of The Ottawa Journal that he had been a KGB agent for 30 years and that he did it for kicks?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: STATUS OF CASE CONCERNING PROFESSOR HAMBLETON
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very familiar with this matter. It is an operation known to the RCMP as Operation Red Pepper. The Department of Justice officials and law officers looked at all the matters that were uncovered by the RCMP that were made known to me, and there was nothing there that would form an adequate basis, in the opinion of justice officials, for a successful prosecution under the Officials Secrets Act. For that reason, no charges were laid under that act.

Will the minister tell the House whether it is government policy to permit certain persons to cavort around with Soviet agents, give them material-and certainly the minister will admit that happened-and yet be completely free of any consequences, when they are actually working against the interests of this country? speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. EAST COAST FISHERIES TREATY-EFFECT OF NON-RATIFICATION

1 do not remember saying, and 1 do not think it is a phrase I use in my vocabulary, "turning fishermen loose". 1 always very cautiously approach this area and this subject by using the expression that we cannot allow the increase of effort on the part of U.S. Fishermen to put us in a position of having a sort of historical right if a new treaty or new arrangements have to be negotiated in case of non-ratification by the U.S. Senate. We approve of their being given a time limit within which to report, and we also approve of the right of each committee, if it wishes to do so, to make public its report when its work is finished, even if Parliament is not sitting at that time. I believe it was also understood that, although there are just five parliamentary task forces set out in this motion, a sixth one is in prospect having to do with trade. It is awaiting the return of the minister concerned so that the terms of reference can be outlined. When a similar motion is made under that subject we shall agree to it as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State, Small Businesses) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASE OF ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
That Bill C-20, to amend the Federal Business Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am happy to introduce in the House today Bill C-20, to amend the Federal Business Development Act, at the second reading stage.
This bill provides two ways to increase the loans of the bank to small businesses. First, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), with the approval of the governor in council, can authorize capital payments to the Federal Business Development Bank not exceeding $475 million, which represents an increase of $275 million over the usual capital ceiling of the bank.
Second, the ratio of the direct liabilities of the bank to its capital will rise from 10 to 12, with the provision that the
Federal Business Development Bank Act governor in council can increase it up to 15. Mr. Speaker, this bill also contains a provision limiting the combined aggregate liabilities and capital of the bank to $3.2 billion, or $1 billion over the present statutory maximum authorized by the act.
This additional $1 billion in the lending power of the bank will be a sufficient temporary measure to allow the bank to fulfil its present mandate for about two more years. As I said in the House during the discussions on the bill to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, this legislation is temporary because the government is undertaking a complete review of all its financial support programs for small businesses. This review should be completed in about 12 to 16 months, and the government will then introduce more comprehensive policy proposals for the future role of the Federal Business Development Bank and other government assistance programs for small businesses.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the last Parliament the previous government had introduced legislation, Bill C-4, aiming at temporarily raising the bank's capitalization. This bill would have allowed the bank to raise from 10 to 12 the ratio of its total direct and contingent liabilities to its capital, with a clause allowing this ratio to be raised up to 15 times the capital. However, for obvious reasons, this bill died on the order paper. The bill 1 introduce today again proposes to raise the ratio, but more important still, it contains an additional clause to allow for injection of new capital in the bank. This provision aimed at increasing the capital of the bank reflects our government's concern to prevent the capital of the bank from becoming overly onerous, because of its composition, for their preferential customers, that is small enterprises.
Mr. Speaker, the Federal Development Bank and its predecessor, the Industrial Development Bank, have played a major role in the government's Financial programs to aid small businesses, and that goes back to 1944. The bill before us will enable the bank to continue filling its mandate of term lender to small businesses who cannot find elsewhere a loan at reasonable conditions.

At this time I should like to highlight some aspects of the bank's activities. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1980, the bank authorized over 16,000 new loans for a total of over $880 million, which is an increase of 36 per cent in the number of customers and 30 per cent in the dollar amount of gross authorizations over the previous fiscal year. At the end of fiscal year 1980, the bank had over 40,000 customers on its books and over $2 billion worth of loans outstanding.
As an indication of the bank's small business orientation, I should like to say that the average size of loan authorized in the latest fiscal year was in the order of $55,000. Furthermore, 90 per cent of the loans made by the bank are for amounts of $ 100,000 or less.
Also the bank provides financial support by making equity investments in small businesses when it is appropriate. At the end of the fiscal year 1980, the bank had investment commit-

May 23, 1980
Federal Business Development Bank Act
ments of approximately $40 million. Although the bank has been active in venture capital financing for only a few years, it is now the largest source of venture capital for small businesses in Canada.
The operations of the bank are national in scope with a network of over 100 offices across Canada and a staff of over 2,200 people. As well, officials of the bank regularly makes visits to many smaller centres, including those centres in remote regions of the country, to ensure that the programs and facilities of the bank are available to entrepreneurs located outside urban centres.
The bank is active in every province and territory. In 1979-1980, 9 per cent of the bank's loan authorizations were made in the Atlantic provinces, 23 per cent in the province of Quebec, 30 per cent in Ontario, 15 per cent in the prairie provinces, the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and 23 per cent in British Columbia.
The bank provides financial assistance to small firms in a broad range of industrial sectors including manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, tourism, agriculture, construction, rental properties, transportation and storage, and service industries. However, the major part of the bank's lending is concentrated in three main industrial sectors. For example, in the fiscal year 1979, loans to the wholesale and retail trade accounted for 34 per cent of the number of loans and 25 per cent of the amount lent. The tourism industry accounted for 20 per cent of loans in terms of number of loans and 24 per cent of the amount lent. For manufacturing, the comparable figures were 19 per cent and 24 per cent respectively.
FBDB loans are usually used to acquire land, buildings and/or equipment to strengthen a firm's working capital position, for the establishment of new businesses and for the acquisition of existing businesses.

Another proof of the bank's commitment to small business is that its financing terms are based on the particular needs of each client. In effect, this means the time frame and schedule of repayment arc determined by the firm's circumstances. Also taken into account are profit potential, working capital requirements and useful life of the assets offered as security. The repayment schedule and instalments are determined according to the seasonal nature of some businesses. In addition, loans can be renegotiated where the borrower cannot meet the terms of the original loan agreement due to unforeseen financial problems. The repayment period can extend from one to 25 years, the average being in the vicinity of 8 years.
In addition to loan programs, the FBDB also has a whole gamut of managing services that are a significant part of its support to small businesses. The best known of the management services offered by the bank is CASE, the counselling assistance to small enterprises. The bank retains some 2,000 retired business men and women with impressive knowledge and experience of a wide spectrum of business activities. These
counsellors use their experience and knowledge to help small entrepreneurs solve their management problems. Counselling assistance is usually given on the client's premises and extends over an average two days. The program's popularity can best be judged by the fact that the number of firms having received assistance over the three-year period ended with fiscal year 1979 trebled over. There were more than 10,000 consultations during fiscal 1979.
The bank also has available a series of training sessions that were used by some 25,000 business people last year. Finally, the bank offers information to entrepreneurs on every assistance program available at various levels of government.
For many years, Mr. Speaker, the Federal Business Development Bank has been a major part of the government's financial programs in support of small business. It is more than that. Through financial services in the form of direct loans, investments and management counselling, training and information services, the Federal Business Development Bank provides a wide variety of services for small businesses.
The bill before the House today provides for a recapitalization of the bank to allow it to continue with its financial activities in support of small businesses.
In concluding my remarks, 1 would again like to remind hon. members of the need to deal with this legislation as expeditiously as possible. The bank has committed the last of its funds it is empowered to raise under its existing authority. Unless legislative relief is forthcoming, the bank will have to curtail its lending activities somewhat. As I indicated earlier, this is only an interim measure sufficient to keep the bank operating for approximately two years, pending the outcome of the government's extensive review of small business financing. There will be ample opportunity for hon. members to review the role of the bank in depth when the government comes forward with its comprehensive proposals for small business financing.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASE OF ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is naturally with some regret that I find myself on this side of the House speaking to a bill which I found to be a very important and necessary bill when I enjoyed the office that the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) currently holds. There will not be an excessive delay on the second reading debate on Bill C-20, to amend the Federal Business Development Bank Act, by my party. We would like to see second reading completed before we begin private members' hour today.
The minister closed his remarks by saying that Bill C-20 was an interim measure. He referred in his opening remarks to the former Bill C-4, which was tabled in the House during the previous Parliament. I remind hon. members that Bill C-20 is substantially different from Bill C-4 which was tabled in the previous Parliament. It is very obvious now that I was dealing with a very dedicated and deliberate president of the treasury
May 23, 1980

board in that we placed great emphasis on the cash flow problems of the federal government. We were making truly, 1 think a magnificent effort to reduce the borrowing needs of the government.
We treated the increase in ratio of from one to ten to one to 12 as an expedient measure to cover the Federal Business Development Bank's needs for the next two years, rather than increasing the capital. 1 realized at the time that increasing the ratio from one to ten to one to 12 increased the cost of borrowing for the bank and that this meant its margin between cost of money and revenue received from lending money was greater. If my memory serves me correctly, their margin of burden on top of cost was something like 4.25 per cent.
To me the Federal Business Development Bank, as I am sure the minister will agree, is the federal government's front line of service to the small and medium enterprise community in Canada. When 1 had the opportunity to speak previously as the minister responsible for this area of activity in Canada, 1 pointed out that this area creates new jobs and delivers risk into the business sector. It is an organization that cannot stand on its own in the private sector. It needs government support because it is a lender of last resort.
The difficult thing with the Federal Business Development Bank is that it is asked to maintain a bottom line or a positive cash flow in its operations. At the same time we want it to fulfil that marginal area of risk out in the business sector.
The federal government delivers millions of dollars into the business community through DREE and other departmental programs, but in terms of serving the borrowers and businesses which are in this marginal area where there is a high degree of risk, and where normal and traditional lenders in the market place say no because of that risk, then the services of this bank come into play.
1 mentioned that Bill C-20 is quite different from the Bill C-4 which was tabled in the last Parliament. The government is not only amending the ratios which the previous bill asked for-that is moving from one to ten to one to 12, with governor in council approval for moving from one to 15-it is also amending or asking for a substantial increase in the capital of the bank. I could not get that request through the last president of the treasury board. It is obvious that the present minister is a real soft touch and that the incumbent President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is a real pussycat.
If I were the president of the Federal Business Development Bank 1, too, would be seeking exactly what the bill before us today proposes. The government seems to have abandoned totally, I guess as a result of February 18, any concern for Conservative principles in management of cash flow, management of debt and the ability to say no to anything. That is the situation with which we are dealing and that is perhaps why I find myself in a difficult position in this debate today.
However, being a believer in the democratic process, I must accept the wisdom and the will of the Canadian electorate and I will try to do the best I can as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to test the wisdom of this bill, while at the
Federal Business Development Bank Act
same time saying that I have great admiration and respect for the officers of the bank, the president of the bank, for the job which this bank performs in our community and for the problem which the Minister of State for Small Businesses has on his desk.
Bill C-20 moves the capital limit from $200 million to $475 million. I seriously question if that move of $275 million is responsible and whether it might even be necessary. Certainly as this bill moves into committee we will be asking for justification of that move of some $275 million in capital.
The key political issue, Mr. Speaker, that we have to deal with in this bill is that Parliament has to decide the degree of subsidy it is prepared to deliver to the Federal Business Development Bank whose mandate requires that it be the lender of last resort. That, again, is what we are dealing with in this bill, as we were in the previous Bill C-4.
The challenge of the bank lies in ensuring that it carries out its expected function at a profit, while taking risks that prudent lenders refuse. The bank also provides extensive educational services, as the minister mentioned in his speech, through its case studies and case counsellors, and delivery of services into regions not normally considered to have economic viability for the private and traditional marketplace lenders. Under its mandate it must therefore provide more services, while maintaining reasonable and stable lending rates.
It is incumbent upon each and every one of us to understand the difficulties that the president and managers of the bank have in working under its mandate, dealing at the perimeters of the marketplace and the market of risk.
The bank also, because of its market and the mandate we place on it, has to deal with and focus on small loans which have a higher percentage of carrying cost and administration cost than large loans. 1 think it is on record that its main competitor in term lending delivery is Roynat, whose average loan, I believe, is something like $320,000 to $330,000. A year ago the Federal Business Development Bank's average loan was in the order of $54,000, and today I believe it has slipped to $47,000. This is a high burden of cost that we have to acknowledge is within the management problem of the bank. We want that situation to exist, however, because that is a service to the marginal activities of the business community that we need.
The bank also has to operate in an environment of voyeurs or "peeping Toms", because the traditional market lenders are always concerned that the bank is stealing customers from them and is playing games with the matter of lender of last resort. The bank has, therefore, also built safeguards into its administration cost and burden, so that it is always in a position to explain or defend itself against that constant criticism that most members of Parliament receive when dealing with disgruntled applicants or borrowers from the Federal Business Development Bank. That is another burden it has to maintain in its management or explanation of its affairs when

May 23, 1980
Federal Business Development Bank Act
it deals politically with members of Parliament or ministers who have disgruntled constituents.
I have received a pile of letters and criticism from colleagues on this side and the other side of the House and from constituents at large in Canada regarding the bank's activities. There could have been a time in the bank's affairs when some of that criticism was justified. At large, however, it was my experience in the short time I was in office that the bank handles itself with a great deal of pride, respect and concern for the positions and conditions under which it has to operate in its mandate.
In most cases 1 know of where there is a criticism of attitude on the part of a regional manager, the senior officers of the bank will move with dispatch to obtain an explanation. 1 would say to all members of the House dealing in this political aspect of the bank's service that they have to remember there is another side to the story. There are always two sides to this type of argument and I would plead with them to get the other side of the story before making serious allegations, keeping in mind, of course, that it is our job to make sure the bank and its personnel operate as a government institution to serve that aspect of the marketplace.
Another burden that does not reflect in the earnings of the bank is the fact that the bank officers and counsellors will often go into applications that have been refused by traditional lenders and will put together a combination of factors to bring that application for a loan into a category of safety with the result that the traditional lenders then want it. The bank has to yield that burden of work to the traditional lender because it is a lender of last resort. That is a cost that we must keep in mind as we discuss this federal government service to the small and medium enterprise sector.
One of the problems that I do not think has been brought to light in the House is the high turnover of credit managers and staff at the bank. 1 think the bank has become a training ground, at high cost to its cash flow and overhead, for credit managers and managers for the traditional lending institutions in Canada. Maybe this is a good thing, but I sympathize with the problems it poses for senior management and the president of the bank.
As the minister is asking for such a large sum of capital in addition to the increased ratio, 1 think we should be moving in and considering-if we can do so at committee stage-lifting the president's salary to a point commensurate with the quality of the job he is doing for the bank. We should increase the salary ratio in order to keep senior officers of the bank so that the quality of delivery of service, considering the difficult management factors they have to deal with, which 1 believe I have explained fairly, is in place. I would urge the minister to take an initiative on this. Perhaps when we go into committee or even in the House, if he winds up this debate, he will confirm that the president's salary will be lifted and that the salary of senior people in the administration of the bank will be lifted to the point that we can offer the bank some stability in terms of staff.
1 would not want to interfere too much with the bank being a training ground to upgrade the financial community at large. 1 think, however, that the market sector is very capable of doing most of its own training. I do not think we should be losing key personnel to it by default or by lagging behind the compensatory levels of the marketplace.
The front line of service that the bank offers the business community is its seminars. These are of good quality and are well received. They should be advertised so that more and more people from the small business sector attend. They have a nucleus of experience that can often avert tragedy and heartbreak brought about by risky enterprises. High quality educational material is published by the bank. The case counselling service is supplemented through the estimates, and this has been expanded. Some day soon we must examine the subsidy made to the case counselling service to satisfy ourselves that it is good value for the money. Personally I think it is.
The bank is moving into the hinterland in outer regions which the traditional lenders do not consider economically viable. It carries the small loans that have a high burden of administrative or initiative costs that other lenders do not want.
I am sure the bank is at a point of crisis today. It needs an expansion of its ceiling of last December. It has gone through a period of nine increases in interest rates over the last year, and has had to face an accelerated rate of bankruptcies. Again, if my memory serves me correctly, we were budgeting for something like 5,800 bankruptcies in Canada, and there was a reserve built in based on that projection. If the figure given to me orally is correct, the actual number has turned out to be around 8,000 bankruptcies.
So, the bank has had to move in with something like $29 million in write-offs-I hope that figure is correct-to cover bankruptcies that the bank had been carrying on its books in categories three and four, which are the categories of loans that have had to face postponement or have been put aside in the reserve with the hope that somehow or other the combination of factors could be put together to move them back to category two, then to category one and eventually be retired.
As we examine the changes and the reasons for the changes in the bank's conditions, which we will be doing in committee, Parliament will have to decide whether the bank is to work on a cost recovery basis or whether it is prepared to subsidize, on an annual average basis, a degree of marginal ventures. The review that the minister speaks of, and it is a very important exercise indeed, has to deal with this. We could perhaps start at committee stage to express concern and perhaps give some input to that aspect of this bill at that time.
I am told by its president that the bank since Bill C-4 has had additional factors to consider and deal with beyond those given to the previous minister of state responsible for the bank. A matching problem has shown up between borrowings and loans. The average term of loan outstanding with the Federal
May 23, 1980

Business Development Bank is eight years, while the roll-over in terms of the bank's debt to the Bank of Canada is on a five-year basis. The portfolios that it has inherited from the Industrial Development Bank it now claims were not properly matched, and this has been an additional burden of cost the bank has had to carry and that has come to light within the last half year. This has cost the bank considerably in light of the nine increases in interest rates over the last year.
1 can remember-going back to the Thirtieth Parliament and to the then Bill C-16, the borrowers depositors act, the one where we started to monkey around with the terms of medium and long-range loans-cautioning the House at that time about this aspect, and my caution subsequently turned out to be right, because the bill was withdrawn. Any time we are dealing with legislation interfering with the term of loans, this is something that we have to be cognizant of, and I think the problem that the bank has is proof of the accuracy of that claim made during the debate on the former Bill C-16.
As a member coming from the private sector 1 often look at FBDB as my window on the banking community and its problems, in the same way that some of us in the House see Petro-Canada as a window on energy industry.
1 am also told that the $100 million increase in capital requested of the last government by the bank did not take into account the venture capital program, and that the venture capital program requires equity because equity should be invested in equity situations. The bank should not be borrowing and creating debt to invest in equity situations. 1 agree totally with that fundamental principle.
There is justification for some increase over the $100 million that it was seeking in terms of increased capital so that it could remain within an 8 to 1 debt-loan ratio, and there is some $75 million of legitimate request in this increase in capital that the minister is asking for. I will remind members again that the minister is asking for an increase in capital of $275 million in addition to a widening of the ratio of from one to ten to one to 12. In this bill the minister is asking for everything one could imagine in terms of expansion. The only thing that saves me from blowing my eyebrows is that there still remains a cap in the bill of $3.2 million in terms of outstanding loans.
I am told the venture capital equity demands on the bank to March 31, 1981, is $50 million and that its budget requires an additional $25 million to build up its venture or equity lending for the next two and a half years. Therefore, I can substantiate $75 million of the minister's request in this bill in that area.
The former president of the treasury board had imposed an attitude of total restraint on his colleagues in cabinet and on presidents of Crown corporations, such as the Federal Business Development Bank. Although it was an option at that time that we increase the capital by $100 million, the general policy of restraint that we were under moved us over from increasing the capital into increasing the ratio from one to ten to one to 12.1 do not know what the situation is, but I think the bank faced very serious problems as we went through nine increases in interest rates, and because its matchings were not in balance added to its cash flow problem and burden. Now that we have
Federal Business Development Bank Act a rapidly decelerating interest rate in the marketplace, 1 would think that loan authorizations to loan lendings would accelerate. Cancellations of approvals through March and April of this year have allowed the bank to still service loans. The high cancellation rate again has added to the bank's administrative burden per loan outstanding. I would think that it is now facing the situation whereby the approvals of applications and the actual delivery of loans would start to accelerate with the new interest rates that are coming into place on the market.
I appreciate that the minister and the president of the bank have time-frames whereby we should be delivering this bill and this authority to them. However, I am wondering if those matching problems they faced as interest rates went up are now offset as interest rates come down. I think we would want to examine that aspect in committee.
One other aspect of the bank's problem, and particularly in a period of rising rates, could be resolved if we had a look in committee at the floating rate principle, and 1 would put on notice now that I think members should be questioning the minister not only on a floating rate as it would apply to the administration of the bank, but a floating rate as a possible benefit to the bank's borrowers, keeping in mind some of the other problems that the bank faced which 1 believe I have outlined today.
The cost of money to the bank is an important issue we should be examining in the committee and that members should consider. 1 understand that since 1975 the average ratio has been eight to one and that the cost of money for the bank fits into that framework. 1 am not sure that 1 remember the exact figure of its major competitor in the term lending field, but 1 think it was operating at a seven to one ratio.
If we accept what the minister has given to us in Bill C-20 with capitalization moving from $200 million to $475 million against a cap on loans of $3.2 million, we find that the bank is trying to move down to a ratio of seven to one so that it can match its cost of money to its major competitor in the marketplace. That cap would be good for about two years of operation, I understand.
I have examined the figures. I see the $75 million of equity required for the next two and a half years for venture capital programs. I see $30 million needed to cover the bankruptcies that it will have to write off in categories three and four. I expect that is a normal degree of risk for a lender of last resort. If we put in $100 million of capital for loans, my arithmetic tells me that would yield an eight to one ratio for the bank which has been their average since 1975. With that rule-of-thumb arithmetic, I would just ask the minister why we have to amend section 31 and increase the ratio from one to ten to one to 12. Why do we not go for a $200 million or $205 million increase on the 200? Would he explain why we need that extra $70 million of capital?
It is important that members understand that he is not asking for cash out of treasury in moving from 200 to 475. What he is asking for and what the bank is asking for is a

Federal Business Development Bank Act
cancellation of debt to the Government of Canada. This brings us into the whole debate of cancelling debt of Crown corporations and playing games with the balance sheet of Canada. I want hon. members to be fully cognizant of what we are doing here. There is an effect to the balance sheet of Canada.
Perhaps 1 am too old-fashioned in my education and conservative way of managing things that have to do with dollars and cash flow, but I get a little disturbed when we start playing games here that the tax collector does not allow in the marketplace. I would like to see that addressed in the minister's reply or at least when we go to committee.
I must say it is not easy for a person schooled and brought up during the depression, working hard and saving every dollar of earnings you can to have a dollar of capital in order to invest and risk in the marketplace, to stand as a responsible member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition on this bill. I think the minister has gone too far. He has asked for more than he needs. I think we should bring the bill back to an increase of $200 million in capital and leave the ratio where it is, at one to ten. 1 put it on record that I would like answers to that in the wind-up speech or in committee.
We have a review coming up that I believe the minister said would be available in something like 16 months. 1 would think that review could probably be brought ahead, but if 16 months is what is needed, that is fine. We should also be acquainted with some of the interim reports of that review, so that we do not get it in one overpowering bundle in terms of any sincere reaction to or criticism of it. As I was starting to say, trying to be a constructive critic schooled in conservative management principles in terms of cash flow, 1 am trying to be as gentle as 1 can in saying to the minister that I think the bill is excessive.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat something I have been saying over and over again on the political platform. 1 guess it is one of the reasons why I stood as a person from the small business community carrying a sense of anger and frustration at what was happening to my tax dollar. Most Canadians do not object to paying taxes in a land like this. I do not object personally. I will even work to encourage a fair share distribution of the wealth of this country.
Where I differ with the progress being made by this government or the approach to that of this government is that they, through the process and bureaucracy of government, are setting taxation levels that are too high for an incentive to remain for the risk-takers in the market place. When that happened all down through history, we have seen the entrepreneurs of countries leave or fall back and rest. We cannot address the problems of this country if we smother the initiative and energy of the entrepreneurs and risk-takers in the business community. The cash flow problems of the treasury are going to mount and accelerate in relation to the degree with which we pull incentives out of the business sector. I am not saying anything new. Every civilization has gone through this cycle, but part and parcel of the dilemma that we are facing in this Parliament is in that destruction of incentives.
As we came through the last election, one of the things I found repeated often by very responsible, intelligent people
May 23, 1980
was that they did not object to the tax or the proposed 18 cent increase on a gallon of gasoline, which was a big election issue. They did not object to that per se as much as they objected to the way the tax revenue is spent, the reckless arrogance and waste of the energy and sweat that goes into producing and delivering a dollar of tax into this treasury.
If we are to create excitement and the creation of wealth in this country, and if we are to keep that level of excitement high, for goodness sake stop the extravagance. Bill C-20 asks for the moon. It asks for more than the bank needs at this point in time, particularly as a very important review is in place. I suggest we start right here in this Parliament, bring this bill back and give the bank what it needs to function properly, but let us not overdo it.
I hope that this second reading debate can be completed before private members' hour today and I look forward to the challenge and the discussion in committee on this bill. May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy to rise this afternoon in the debate on Bill C-20, to amend the Federal Business Development Bank Act. 1 listened very carefully and enjoyed the comments made by the minister detailing the perceived benefits of the act and how it has been very, very helpful to small businessmen in Canada from one end to the other. 1 am pleased to know that its benefits were distributed relatively equally across this country.
1 also listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). His comments covered many of the specifics of the bill and focused on the amending ratios, the increase in capitalization being provided for the bank and the concept of debt cancellation which has been involved. Since he went through those specifics, 1 will restrict my comments to items other than those in an effort to
May 23, 1980

ensure that his bill receives speedy passage and that we get it into committee and deal with it at the earliest opportunity.
I recognize that the Federal Business Development Bank is really a lender of last resort. What it does, in my mind, is indicate a very important and crucial trend which has developed in Canadian economics in the last number of years. I want to focus some of my comments this afternoon on that trend. I suspect that many members of the House are not aware of what the importance of this bill indicates to us here and to Canadians generally.
I was both surprised and, I suppose, somewhat alarmed at the comments made by the hon. member for Capilano. I was surprised at his recognition of the role that the federal government is playing in the private enterprise sector and that he should extol the benefits of this development bank. I was somewhat alarmed not at the comments he was making but at the fact that his comments were so accurate in that the reason we are discussing this bill this afternoon is partly because of the failure of our financial institutions in this country.
1 want to take a moment to put this discussion into context by suggesting that during the 1950s, 1960s and perhaps even the early 1970s there was a sense of economic optimism about the land. People saw an endless range of opportunities for those with entrepreneurial interests and instincts. Canada was a very worth-while place in which to be investing. Education at our colleges and universities across the country virtually guaranteed employment in the career or profession of one's choosing. Training of one kind or another in the occupational sector virtually guaranteed a job, increasing employment opportunities were found across Canada, and, of course, this very positive climate manifested itself in an increasing willingness of people to get involved in the business sector, and particularly for the small entrepreneur, the small businessman, to become involved in an enterprise where he or she was eventually his or her own boss.
1 would be surprised if there were many members in the House representing all parts of Canada who have not at one time or other been involved or have wanted to be involved in business, who had a dream, an aspiration to take that initiative and assist in the development of our fine country. During the period of the 1950s, 1960s and early 1970s, funding for ventures was available, new ideas were encouraged and nurtured, risks were relatively minimal and so were failures.
However, unfortunately the experiences of the 1970s have essentially systematically destroyed this optimism. There is an increasing air of uncertainty in our country today, a feeling that our future will not necessarily be a better one, that the world of the 1980s and 1990s will not necessarily be better than the world we have in Canada today. Obviously confidence has been reduced.
This has led to increasing risks to many small businessmen and small entrepreneurs. Here are individuals who are experiencing at this time shortages in capital, expertise and information data, recognizing daily the growing imperfections
Federal Business Development Bank Act in the marketplace. Indeed it is a time of transition, a time when our economy is experiencing a transformation. Small has now become rather precarious, small has become rather uncertain and small has certainly become risky. To survive in Canada today as an entrepreneur it is certainly in your favour to be very big to survive, let alone to grow. In order to have access to more capital, to have access to resources, to manpower and to information, you must be big.
I suggest that large companies have achieved today a significant advantage in our system. Probably this advantage is most clearly demonstrated in our taxation system. Not so much in our rates of taxation, but when you examine the taxes paid by the large corporations and those paid by our small business companies you see a substantial difference, which indicates clearly that the large companies have a significant advantage.
1 suggest that this points to an inherent contradiction today in our economic system. Today we possess essentially a certain image of tens of thousands of small businesses across the country-and indeed they are there-accounting for something in the neighbourhood of 40 per cent of Canada's employment. Yet when you examine the situation carefully it becomes obvious that power lies with the large corporation, that power lies with the large multinational corporation. We have today a situation where Canadians possess an illusion, an impression, of an economy dominated by small entrepreneurs and small businessmen.
Of course, we extol the virtues of the small businessman, the small community and the small town. We say that small is best, that small is easy to comprehend, yet this is inconsistent with the realities of the 1980s. Today small business is being excluded from the marketplace. One of the most obvious examples of this is where small business is being excluded from the traditional sources of funding. Banks are becoming increasingly hesitant to lend to the small, higher risk entrepreneur. Banks, the traditional lending institutions, desiring more and more security, find that security in the large company incorporation.
Just yesterday in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, representatives of Canada's banks indicated that banks were not prepared to finance small livestock processors unless those processors could use someone else's property for collateral. To me it indicates the extent to which the traditional funding institutions are going in this country. How many of us in this chamber are able to go into a bank and use someone else's property as collateral, as the banks demand? That is what the banks were demanding in committee yesterday in an effort to finance the livestock processor, packing plants and so on. It is too risky for the chartered banks so therefore they are prepared to cut off their funding.
Due to this elimination of funds, a financial crisis has emerged and is continuing to emerge in Canada. During these years when, goodness knows, we need Canadian investors, when we need to encourage new ideas in the economic sector, when we need to nurture new approaches and ask for new
1366

May 23, 1980
Federal Business Development Bank Act methods and techniques, the traditional funding sources are being reduced or eliminated.
So it begs the question: Who comes to the rescue during these times? Indeed, who comes to the rescue are the provincial and federal governments of Canada. I ask members to reflect on that, particularly those who have been here for some years, and to ask how many programs the federal government had in the 1950s to assist the small businessman and small entrepreneur. Probably one could count those programs on one hand. Yet today as we begin the 1980s, if one were to examine carefully the variety of programs available to the small investor and small businessman, one would find in excess of 400 federal programs, let alone programs in the provincial sector providing encouragement and support to small businessmen. On my desk the other day was a notice from British Columbia listing support of the small business sector through assistance to the small enterprise program. There were pages and pages of small businesses, some manufacturing utility trailers, others manufacturing mobile homes, others manufacturing hydraulic components, people prepared to try new ideas and to take a leadership role in developing Canada's economy.
As the hon. member for Capilano indicated, the private sector interested in venture capital, interested in risk capital, must now look to government, not to the chartered banks of Canada, the traditional lending institutions. The $3.5 billion of capital in our Federal Business Development Bank to be made available to small business demonstrates a failure in our financial capital markets. It demonstrates a failure in our chartered banks, in our trust companies and in our sales finance companies, to provide much needed risk venture capital to the small entrepreneur.
A few days ago we heard discussed in this chamber credit unions and caisses populaires in the province of Quebec which have received a considerable impetus in the last decade and have experienced considerable growth. 1 would suggest that one of the reasons for their success and their tremendous growth in the last decade has been the fact that since they do not lend to corporations, they are essentially providing funding to the single proprietorships, the single businessmen, to the partnerships, to enable this much needed risk capital to enter our economy.
In the end, the private financial sector is failing. It is letting Canadians down at a time when creativity and innovation is necessary, at a time when the frontiersmen of our business community must be opening up new territories to meet the challenges of the 1980s and 1990s. Because traditional funding is too risky, it is not available and the private sector must now depend upon institutions such as the Federal Business Development Bank.
We support Bill C-20, and at the same time we recognize the glaring failure of our chartered banks. We recognize that Bill C-20 provides an opportunity for the federal government now to step in and provide that leadership, for the federal
government to step in and rekindle that spirit, to provide those new options, and to put Canadians back to work.
I want to end my short discussion this afternoon by suggesting as a new member of Parliament that I feel, in considering legislation such as Bill C-20, we are called upon to make decisions without having adequate information. A number of questions ought to be posed. I should like to pose just a few of them for the hon. minister to reflect upon perhaps in his response later this afternoon or to examine when we get into committee.
Why has the FBDB lost money over the past year? What are the real reasons behind that loss? Is there a clear concept of the purpose and the mandate of the Federal Business Development Bank? Why was the staff turnover in this past year so vast? When the bank is losing money as it is, why is it going ahead with spending an additional $35 million or considering a new head office? Has there been a comprehensive review of the bank's operations, focusing on such things as the bank's borrowing policies in terms of its sources of capital? Have the bank's lending practices been examined adequately? What is the expertise of the bank's personnel?
Just so that 1 am not misunderstood, I concur with the comment of the hon. member for Capilano when he recognized the commitment and ambition of those responsible for the bank and the efforts they have made. I might add that these efforts were very positive. I want to emphasize the fact that they have a staff in excess of 2,000 across the country, and perhaps most important of all, they provide that much-needed management advice, introducing management skills to so many of those people who are interested in beginning business ventures. The expertise and the quality of the people they have providing that service must be commended. Looking at perhaps some of the crucial personnel within the bank itself, are we confident that the necessary expertise and background is always in the right place at the right time? I recognize that these are very difficult questions, but nevertheless they are questions that must be addressed.
In closing, I must say that our party certainly supports this bill. In a sense we feel that it is a shame the traditional financial institutions have essentially let us down in terms of providing much-needed venture capital. I am pleased to see that in fact the federal government is leading the way through this expanded bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASE OF ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make some remarks during this debate on Bill C-20, an act to amend the Federal Development Bank Act. This morning, my colleague the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) already expounded to hon. members the details and the main objective of this bill. He also released some details regarding the activities of the bank.
During the period of time allotted to me I intend to stress the role of the bank in the development of the short-term loan
May 23, 1980

market for small and medium-size businesses in Canada and to add some observations to the remarks made by the minister regarding other activities of the bank in the field of management.
Mr. Speaker, as we all know the Federal Business Development Bank was created in October, 1974, to succeed the Industrial Development Bank which was founded in 1944. 1 think that when we created the FBDB we brought it closer to its customers. It acted like the Industrial Development Bank which had been a pioneer in the field of term loans in Canada. The success of both institutions was to a very large extent an important factor in building and expanding a term loan market for small businesses, as 1 said earlier, not by a governmental or public institution, but by a number of financial institutions of the private sector.
Actually, a great many customers of many of these private loan companies are former employees and customers of the bank whose businesses achieved viability thanks, in many cases, to the support of the FBDB or its predecessor. Although it is rather easy to determine the activities of the bank which will directly assist small businesses, and I will speak briefly about it in a few minutes, it is almost impossible to measure the real contribution of the bank as far as the development of private loan services for small businesses is concerned. 1 would like to point out that often disregarded substantial contribution of the bank to private financial institutions which, as you know, represent the most important source of loans to small businesses. It is an indication of the government commitment to co-operate with financial circles and other groups and individuals so as to initiate steps to help small businesses. This should reassure the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) who this morning was concerned about the growing presence of the government or governmental banking institutions in the economic system.

While there have been positive and constructive developments in private financial markets, the Federal Business Development Bank continues to play an active and innovative role in the provision of financing to small businesses. For example, in recent years the bank has made private lenders aware that it is prepared to consider joint or co-financing arrangements on loan proposals which the private lender, for one reason or another, is not prepared to finance entirely on its own. Thus, I commend the banks for this initiative to develop and expand the small business term-lending market in Canada. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, during the past five years ending March 31, 1980, the Federal Business Development Bank has lent almost $3 billion to more than 55,000 small businesses in Canada. In addition, since its establishment, over 75 per cent of the loans granted by the bank are for amounts up to $50,000 and this indicates its attitude towards small businesses. To show how
Federal Business Development Bank Act much it is aware of the needs of small businesses, the bank has decentralized its loan activities to an appreciable extent.
Most loans are now approved by regional branches or offices, which also considerably shortens the time necessary to process the applications and advise the applicants of the decisions. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, my own constituency benefited from this decentralization a few years ago, which has made the Federal Business Development Bank more accessible.
The branch of the FBDB in Valleyfield, where 1 live, serves the counties of Beauharnois, Chateauguay, Huntingdon, Vau-dreuil and Soulanges. This branch, as far as I know, has been in existence since November, 1976. Whoever considers the evolution of its operations realizes the interests of its customers. As of March 31, 1979, the Valleyfield branch had 152 stores, individuals and firms as customers with a total commitment of $8.2 million. One year later, it had 201 customers with a total commitment of $12.9 million. For the information of hon. members, I should add that during the 12-month period ended March 31, 1980, there were 109 loans authorized amounting to $7.3 million. The average loan for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1980, is $67,000, which means that, fundamentally and in practice, the branch of the Federal Business Development Bank which serves our area really helps small business.
Once again, in an effort to allay the fears of the hon. member for Capilano the rate of penetration of that branch in our region is 6 per cent, which means that only 6 per cent of the businesses probably cannot find the financing needed from ordinary or conventional banks, that only 6 per cent of the 2,549 businesses in our area are served by the bank, but at least those people are helping the economy in our part of the country. 1 feel it is desirable, not only that the Federal Business Development Bank should continue its slow but sure assistance, but that it should be helped to do even more, and offer more and better services, and even perhaps continue to offer risk capital.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to come back to more general considerations, during the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1979, I would say that over 40 per cent of all loans granted by the Federal Business Development Bank were used for capital expenditures including land, buildings and equipment. Small businesses are also trying to get assistance from the bank to increase their working capital. Proper financing of the working capital can be a particularly important element of business especially these days when high interest rates are for the small business that is growing rapidly. The bank also grants loans to facilitate changes of ownership, which period is often a difficult one in the evolution, progress or development of a business. Changing owners can also mean adding a new one at the same time.

May 23, 1980
Federal Business Development Bank Act
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with another important activity of the bank, namely, management services for small business. To that end, I shall start with the conclusions of the study on the financial problems of small businesses, which was made before the Federal Business Development Bank was set up, and which revealed that one of the big problems of small businessmen is that of management aptitudes or talents. To meet that need the responsibilities of the Federal Business Development Bank were expanded in order to offer small business management services in addition to financial services.
So those management services include consultation, training and information services. Some of them were started by the Industrial Development Bank itself within the framework of its normal activities in the small business area which expanded following actions taken on an ad hoc rather than a planned basis. However, with the establishment of the Federal Business Development Bank, those activities became a statutory responsibility of the bank, and they were considerably expanded later. Consultation services are offered through CASE the Counselling Assistance to Small Enterprises program. Under this program the bank hires retired managers as advisers to help small businessmen solve their management problems for a minimal fee.	'
The advisers are selected for their competence, their experience in the area in which the customer company operates. The bank can presently call upon about 2,000 advisers for a wide choice of assignments. In the fiscal year 1980, the bank completed more than 14,000 assignments. The program was well received and it is highly regarded. It is interesting to note that the majority of CASE customers do not borrow money from the bank. In other words, the service is also extended to those whose financial position is already fairly secure.
The second part of the bank's management services deals with the promotion of sound management practices for owners or managers of small businesses through management training. It is one thing to help someone set up the management of his business by way of a temporary program, but without the possibility of sharpening the business acumen of his staff the program falls short of the stated objective. Therefore, the bank offers training by way of courses, seminars and other meetings. During the 1980 fiscal year, more than 25,000 businessmen have attended approximately 1,700 seminars held by the bank on matters relating to commercialization, taxation, bookkeeping and cost control. In the framework of its management training, the bank has also developed a number of 30-hour courses which it offers to provincial and territorial authorities in charge of education. This material is used to train adults in community colleges and elsewhere and is also meant for people in charge of small businesses or those who intend to go into business for themselves.
Mr. Speaker, the third part of the bank's management services consists of giving information with respect to business support programs at all levels of government. This objective
has been met through the setting up of new branches in rural areas across the country. Last year, bank offices were responsible for more than 90,000 client contacts. The bank also publishes a series of brochures on business management entitled "Minding Your Own Business" as well as a quarterly bulletin "Small Business News", and also makes available a lot of information on specialized services from various other departments and in particular the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. These publications deal with matters of interest to small business and have an extensive distribution. Moreover, each of the bank's offices houses a reference library allowing small business to have easy access to works of interest.

The Federal Business Development Bank is a major part of the government's financial support program for small business. Its leadership and innovation has contributed significantly to the development of the private term lending market in Canada for small businesses. But the bank is much more than that. In addition to its financial services, the bank provides, as I said previously, a wide range of management services in support of small businesses.
The breadth of the bank mandate is a reflection of the government's commitment of support to a viable and growing small business sector. The bill in front of us is a clear indication of the government's direction in this area, the right direction. I take great pleasure in supporting this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today to speak in favour of Bill C-20, to increase the lending ability of the Federal Business Development Bank. This is my first speech in this House, and 1 would ask for your indulgence and that of hon. members opposite while I place on the record some of the traditional remarks which a member makes on the occasion of his first speech. I can assure this House that they will be brief and that I will then go on to discuss the bill before us.
1 would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to carry my congratulations to Madam Speaker on her appointment. I feel that it is an honour that she richly deserves and I am sure that she will acquit herself in the chair with dignity and fairness, the same dignity and fairness which we have come to expect from the Speakers of this House.
It is an honour and a privilege for me to represent the riding of Simcoe North. For several years my riding was represented by Dr. Philip Bernard Rynard, and his service on behalf of his constituents is a legend in my riding.

Hear, hear!
May 23, 1980

left his mark in Parliament, as he has on the riding of Sirncoe North.
Following in his footsteps is quite a challenge, and I welcome that challenge. I know that this Elouse will be saddened to hear that Dr. Rynard suffered a stroke the day before he was to campaign for me in the last election, but he continues to progress and has recently left hospital. speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING INCREASE OF ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
The riding of Sirncoe North is as diverse as this nation. The townships of Mara, Rama, Orillia, Oro, Medonte, Matchedash, Tay and Tiny are rich in farmland, forest and water, but richest of all in people. The city of Orillia and towns of Midland and Penetanguishene are strong and vibrant parts of the riding. The riding contains people from English and French background strengthened by immigrants from many lands. The economy of Sirncoe North is mixed and that is its strength.
Sirncoe North riding is comprised of farmers, skilled tradesmen, entrepreneurs, tourist operators, store owners, professionals, civil servants and retired people, all of whom rub shoulders throughout the riding. I have lived in Sirncoe North since 1969. We have known triumphs there and some tragedies, but we have come to know that Sirncoe North is a riding rich in people who are Canadian every day of their lives.
Now 1 would like to turn to Bill C-20. The role of the Federal Business Development Bank in financing Canadian small businesses is well known to this House. Its role in counselling small business through its branches and seminars, which it carries on throughout the country, is important to the concept of helping small business to develop in Canada and entrepreneurs to develop management skills. The provision of management consulting services to small business is also important because small business often cannot afford to hire this expertise on its own and which the Federal Business Development Bank makes available at a reasonable rate.
I am pleased to learn that the bank is continuing to take an active part in financing businesses engaged in manufacturing and tourism in Canada, particularly in Ontario. I note that in the nine months ending December 31, 1979, the number of loans in Ontario increased 58 per cent and that their value increased 61 per cent compared to the same period last year. We need such loans. We need the bank activity to foster continued growth in the province of Ontario. We intend to go on maintaining our position as the cornerstone of confederation by manufacturing, employing people, and by good, old-fashioned hard work in the province of Ontario.
It is not my intention to fill the record with a litany of facts and figures designed to prove that my research is equal to that of the minister's or other hon. members. The minister brought forward the facts and figures quite adequately. My colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), reviewed them and I think we have enough statistics on the record.
Federal Business Development Bank Act
We are sent to Parliament to represent the views of our constituents. I wish to place on the record some concerns which 1 feel adequately reflect the viewpoint of the people of Sirncoe North, particularly small business, with respect to the Federal Business Development Bank and this particular amendment. 1 want to talk about what happens to the money after the bank receives it. I want to touch upon the bank's role as a lender of last resort, the image that the bank has with small business, the cost of completing a loan, branch discretion limit, what 1 call the approval-disapproval time lag, and the availability of branches.
It could be suggested that these are matters for committee, but I feel that they are important to the public and small business and that they should be brought forward in this House. I feel comfortable discussing the bill from the standpoint of the borrower, perhaps more so than 1 do from the standpoint of the bank, because I was often, if not in the borrower's shoes, in the shoes beside the borrower as either a chartered accountant or a lawyer. So the loans, guarantees, financial statements, collateral security and related problems are not unknown to me.
1 would also point out that my comments are not the result of dissatisfaction with any particular branch; I think they reflect somewhat the feelings of the public. The small businessman feels that the Federal Business Development Bank should be a lender of last resort. The bank makes that claim. The chartered banks, trust companies and other financial institutions make a profit and report to their shareholders. The FBDB is viewed as a branch of government which has as its principle the provision of assistance to small businessmen who do not qualify for loans with chartered banks or other such institutions because he may have a lack of business experience on equity, or he has an unstable market, a new product or any of the other reasons which would make the ordinary bank on the corner nervous. That is how the general public views the FBDB.
The general public expects the FBDB to take a higher risk than the chartered bank. I believe the public feels that the bank should have a higher bad debt ratio than a chartered bank. It is expected to lose money. Perhaps that is a strange thing to say, but we must understand that the FBDB must take those risks and lose money in some cases.

much that it has used up in five years all the money that was allotted to it by the last Parliament. That is why it is back here again to get more money so it can continue in the future to do as remarkable a job as it has done in the past.

Mr. Speaker. I very much welcome this opportunity to join in the debate on the amendment to the Federal Business Development Bank, Bill C-20, now before us. I would like to make it known from

the beginning that I support the amendment and encourage its speedy passage. Also, 1 would like to say that my general impression of FBDB is a good one. First of all, as 1 have stated, I welcome the amendment before us today. It represents a welcome recognition of the very important role that small business plays in the total economy of Canada. When I say small business, 1 mean "small' in a relative sense. I know FBDB can and does loan very significant amounts of money to larger businesses. However, in reviewing the bank's annual report for 1979, I could not help but notice that two-thirds of the approved loan applications were made for amounts of $50,000 or less. I think it is safe to assume that when you talk about loans of this amount, you are generally talking about assisting small business. While 1 concede that the scope of the FBDB goes beyond merely assisting small business, it is this sector of the economy which I am most concerned about and wish to address. 1 would like to turn my attention to some of these issues.
When you look at the mandate of the Federal Business Development Bank, you quickly see that its intent was to create an organization which would provide financial assistance to businesses which could not get financing elsewhere on reasonable terms and conditions. In other words, it was set up to be a bank specializing in last resort financing.
However, I am concerned that the bank may be too conservative-if you will pardon the expression-in its lending practices. If this indeed is the case, then it could be argued, with justification, that it is not fulfilling the terms of its mandate.
I am the first person to concede that attempting to determine if this is the case, is a very arbitrary matter. It depends on the criteria you use and what your own opinion is of "too conservative". However, I suggest that this is not a new complaint and may never really be settled to everyone's satisfaction.
In a speech delivered on April 9 of this year by Mr. Peter E. Quinn of industry, trade and commerce to the Canadian Advanced Technology Association, he addressed this kind of concern as it relates to the enterprise development program. it is my contention that determining what percentage of issued loans turn bad is an appropriate yardstick to use in passing judgment on how timid the bank is. If this figure is indicative of the bank's failure rate, then I am of the opinion

Again, I wish to restate that trying to determine if this claim is justified is a very arbitrary, subjective judgment. Nonetheless, it is a consideration which is fundamental to the operation of the bank if it is to carry out its mandate accurately.
It may be useful to compare this 1 per cent loss rate to other programs of a similar nature. Although it is not by any means a mirror image of FBDB, the enterprise development program could be used as a comparison. In the speech just referred to, Mr. Quinn notes that EDP's loss percentage in its field of jurisdiction approximates some 17 per cent. Along the same lines, DREE has a failure rate of close to 10 per cent and its mandate does not specifically refer to the department as being a clearing-house for business looking for last resort financial assistance.
If the FBDB is too timid and thus is not completely fulfilling its mandate as I have suggested, then we must question the causes of this tendency. Part of the problem may be found in the fact that many of the people employed by the bank have come from private sector lending institutions. Their training in the private sector has made them understandably leery of risk loan ventures, and for obvious reasons. Once this philosophy is instilled, it is understandably difficult to reject. To come from a chartered bank, which is not favourably disposed to extending loans to businesses turned down everywhere else, it must be trying on credit officers at FBDB to remember that risky ventures are the rule, and certainly not the exception, of their clients.
Another possible reason for this limited risk mentality that has often been levelled at the FBDB may be further compounded by the fact that since 1979 the bank has begun to raise money on the private money markets. Obviously the bank has to recognize the fact that it raises money on the private market and has to temper any excesses in lending money with the responsibility it has to take into account the raising and repaying of these obligations. Therefore, one can easily sympathize with the FBDB for being caught in a difficult position.
These problems could be addressed without compromising the intent and purpose of the bank. The following ideas are submitted as possible alternatives. First, it is important that those involved in processing applications be made aware that the FBDB's mandate includes high risk. It is an approach designed to recondition their thinking, and must be a goal of management.
