Mr. Speaker, U welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-20, which proposes to amend the Federal Business Development Bank Act.
When the Federal Business Development Bank was established in 1974, its mandate was clearly stated. The new bank was to give particular consideration to the needs of small businesses and to lend money in a responsible manner to those
for whom financing was not available-and 1 underline this- under reasonable terms and conditions from private lenders.
Now, after five years of operation, we are told that increased activity within the business community, and particularly the small business community, has placed unprecedented demands on the Federal Business Development Bank's financial resources. The bank faces the prospect of reaching the statutory limits of its capital and borrowing power within a very few short months.
Like so many of us in these hard times, the Federal Business Development Bank is running out of money. Bill C-20 would increase the Federal Business Development Bank's borrowing power from a factor of ten to 12 times the capital of the corporation.
Without this increase, as has been said earlier, the Federal Business Development Bank would only be able to lend an amount of money equal to the repayment of existing loans. This would cause the bank's loan approvals to drop to one-third of their current level. On the average the bank assists 1,500 small and medium-sized businesses every month. If its loan approvals drop to one-third, well over 1,000 Canadian business operations will be left without funding.
From the outset I want to go on the record as being in support of the proposed increase. I support this increase in spite of some of the criticisms which I will speak about later. I am willing to encourage speedy passage of this legislation through the House so that many Canadian businesses will not be denied access to a vital credit source.
The use of credit is a valuable and essential tool within the small business community. This is particularly true in my constituency of Okanagan North. We are a constituency of small businesses. By way of example, the owner of an independent farm equipment dealership told me the other day that his company's sales volume has doubled every year for the last four consecutive years. He also said that it would have been entirely impossible for him to do this had he not taken advantage of various credit sources, including the Federal Business Development Bank, to buy the inventory and build the facilities he needed to service his customers properly.
Credit, as we all know, is essential to the survival of the small business person, and yet obtaining adequate financing from private lenders is one of the most serious difficulties facing small business firms and, as has been said before in this debate, especially those firms starting new operations.
The Federal Business Development Bank, according to the statistics we have heard, is estimated to assist in the start-up of over 2,000 enterprises per year in Canada. When we add to this the fact that those 2,000 businesses are responsible for the creation or preservation of some 36,000 jobs, it is hard to argue against allowing the corporation to continue lending on a business-as-usual basis.
The Federal Business Development Bank performs a very important function in fostering the development of private enterprise in this country. Private enterprise makes up the heart of the Canadian economy. One of the primary objectives

of at least the people on this side of the House is to ensure that private enterprise in Canada, comprising our small business people, is given every opportunity to take advantage of their individual initiative to grow and prosper.
1 believe it is the responsibility of this House to create an environment which will facilitate growth and development- not to hinder or overwhelm it. It has been said many times, Mr. Speaker, but I believe the figures deserve repetition and reinforcement, that the 1.2 million small businesses in Canada employ over two-thirds of our work force. One point two million business owners and two-thirds of our work force deserve more than just the cursory attention of this House. Small business preserves competition and efficiency in the market place. It also provides more opportunities for less skilled workers.
This vital sector of the Canadian economy wants and needs a small business policy which will create an environment in which individual creativity can flourish.
I will confess, Mr. Speaker, that it was with some disappointment, but certainly not surprise, that 1 watched the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appoint his cabinet. The policy to which I refer, however, is the apparent effort of some local branches to compete-and compete fiercely-for existing business, which the usual financial resources could handle. It appears they compete by advertising and also by establishing local branches in prime office locations-in the so-called high rent districts, in new and modern first floor walk-in offices, for which undoubtedly they pay the highest rent in the area.
By way of example, the Federal Business Development Bank opened a branch office in the town in which I reside, Vernon, B.C., some time ago on the second floor of a fully adequate building, about a block off the main thoroughfare-not prime office space certainly, but adequate for a government corporation which, presumably, was not competing in the open marketplace, but was, in reality, a second-line source of credit.
There should be no need for a great, successful corporate image on the main street on behalf of a federal bank. One would think their needs would be restricted to adequate floor space, a telephone number, an address in the phone book, and sufficient identification on the outside of the building. One would have thought this adequate, and I agree with the hon. member for Simcoe North when he says there should be a branch in every constituency, but not on the main street, not competing with the major banks.
However, in a very short time, the Federal Development Bank in my community was advertising and calling for bids for new office space in a prime location. That particular branch succeeded in its endeavours and now has new office space in a prime location, with presumably higher rent, at more expense to the taxpayer. It is all very nice and it looks very well in Vernon, but I do not think it was necessary.
I hasten to say, Mr. Speaker, it is no answer to say that the cost of this high-class building or the rent of that building is covered in the bank's profits, since any excessive and unnecessary costs will certainly result in higher interest rates and less profit, and a higher rent would eventually cost more to the people who use the service and more to the individual taxpayer.
I can only presume this kind of empire building is carried on throughout the country, and I know there has been some criticism of it. I say that if it is an active policy of the bank, it should be discouraged by the head officers of the corporation as soon as possible. I believe there can be no justification whatsoever for this kind of ego trip on the part of the bank.
I would now like to discuss another practice which, if it exists as a bank policy, should be discontinued immediately.

May 23, 1980
Federal Business Development Bank Act
I presume the bank follows normal banking practices in the granting of loans to its customers. But, of necessity, if it is to fulfil its role of providing a supplementary or secondary line of credit for small business it must, of course, relax some of the usual rules of credit which are enforced by banks or other first line credit granting institutions. So far so good. However, in granting credit the Federal Development Bank almost always takes as security a debenture on the assets of the business which is obtaining the loan.
The debenture is a form used by the bank, as most members of this House will be aware-if they are not they should be- which grants the bank the right in the case of default, to appoint a receiver of the assets of that business, and to take over and sell off all the assets of the business at the discretion of the local bank manager. This, of course, is not an unusual practice, Mr. Speaker; it is also followed by those in private industry when they feel that the type of loan they are giving requires exceptional security. I find no fault with this procedure. However, it is my understanding that this security is taken by the Federal Business Development Bank far more often than by charter banks, at least this is true in my experience.
I might also add, as the hon. member for Simcoe North said, that the Federal Business Development Bank requires documentation that this is far more detailed and extensive and, correspondingly, more expensive than the chartered banks. Thus, while the interest rates may seem to be competitive with those of the chartered banks, all too often the cost of the loan is very much higher as compared to the cost of loans from chartered banks and other private financial institutions. In my opinion, in many cases this documentation is excessive and unnecessary. But this is not the main thrust of my criticism, this is not the real reason I bring the matter up- although these are important matters of practice which the officers of the bank should look to and look to immediately.
The matter which most concerns me is the charge which has been made to me, and which I believe should be answered by the bank, that many of the officers of the Federal Business Development Bank, in their various branches throughout Canada, are too quick to call in their loan when the creditor defaults. By their policy the Federal Business Development Bank-it has been charged-too often entices the business person to borrow too much money and to overextend himself. In doing so, the bank does not provide that business person with sufficient working capital over a sufficient period of time.
In other words, the Federal Business Development Bank does not provide a reasonable repayment plan to enable the borrower to start to overcome his difficulties, to turn his business into a paying proposition, to turn it around to enable him to commence paying off his loan. Instead, at the first sign of default, the bank comes pouncing in, as it were, seizing all assets and the business. In short, the charge is that all too often the Federal Business Development Bank entices the business person to borrow more money than that person
should, and then the business owner finds he cannot meet the terms of the loan. Then the bank moves quickly, decisively, and, it appears, without any regard for the welfare of the small business owner. It calls in his loan and proceeds to take over the business by means of an administrator, selling the assets and discontinuing the business.
The small business owner went to the bank in good faith. He took this loan, he mortgaged his assets, and now he finds himself without a business, without a livelihood, without assets, probably with substantial personal debts and facing bankruptcy, if not already in it. Again my charge is that too often the Federal Business Development Bank entices the businessman into bankruptcy. I do not know whether they do this because of the overeagerness of small bank managers attempting to compete in the market and attempting to build up their records. I do not know whether it is done because the manager himself does not have sufficient business experience to know what size of loan is required in the particular business he is financing, or whether he does not know the period of time or the amount of capital the small businessman requires in order to turn his business around. Whatever it is, I think the record is clear.
I have witnessed the scenario which I have painted here. I do not believe, and I know, that it is not an isolated incident. It is a policy which should be condemned by this Parliament. I would ask the minister to assure the House that my complaint will be brought to the attention of those in the bank whose responsibility it is to ensure that this policy is discontinued forthwith. As I said, I support the early passage of this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to say a few words in support of Bill C-20. Along with my colleagues, 1 certainly realize the importance of this bill. In fact I believe on April 15, just after the House started sitting, I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) when this bill would be brought in because it was brought to my attention by several people interested in borrowing from the Federal Business Development Bank that the funds had dried up and that there would be no money there until new, additional funds were voted by Parliament. I am delighted to know that Parliament now has a bill before it and that this bill will receive second reading today.
I listened with interest to the comments of many of my colleagues on both sides of the House. They have quoted all the necessary statistics and figures, so I would just be repeating them. I come from the small rural riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka where we do not have a branch of the bank. With all due respect, I appreciate the comment that it would be nice to have a branch in every riding in Canada, but 1 am realistic enough to know that money does not grow on trees. Of much more importance than a branch in every riding is to have the money available in every riding and to have officers of the branch there. I have found the officers with whom I deal most co-operative and helpful. One officer with whom I deal is
May 23, 1980

located to the north of my riding in North Bay, and the other is located in the branch to the south, in Barrie.
Along with a great many other members of Parliament, I have been approached by applicants for federal business development loans. We are told by the applicants that we are all-powerful, that all we have to do is tell the bank to lend them the money and the bank will. Of course, I am well aware that it is far from that. 1 have told every one of these applicants that, first and foremost, I have been informed in a roundabout way that the bank takes a very dim view of a member of Parliament trying to wield a very big stick on the knowledgeable people. I told them that it was up to them to sell their business or prospective business to the branch. 1 said that 1 would try to open the doors for them, but they must have a financial statement ready, they must have the knowhow. Also 1 told them that when they have done this, it is up to them, and if 1 could assist in any other way, I will do so. 1 want to commend the many branch managers, or the ones with whom 1 deal, for their courtesy and their endeavouring to help get the loans through.
Some of us think that they do not move too fast, but 1 spoke to one bank manager this morning who stated that his average was 45 to 60 days. That is a pretty good batting average, if it takes 45 to 60 days from the time the application comes in until the loan is finally processed. In some cases it could even be quicker. In a good many cases I am aware that the fault lies with the applicant himself. He goes into the branch without a financial statement or does not give the full story to the branch manager. Therefore he cannot expect to get the "okay" right away.
As has been mentioned time and again, the Federal Business Development Bank is the lender of last resort. I am well aware of that because I also wear the shoes of a borrower. Some years ago I had to enlarge the premises I had in Burk's Falls and build a small building. Therefore 1 went with my hat in hand to the Royal Bank of Canada. While they did not throw me out on my posterior into the street, they would not give me the money. Then 1 went to the Federal Business Development Bank, and after some time the loan was approved at the peak interest rate, which did not please me too well. That was approximately ten years ago and the rate was 10 per cent. Right after that I think the interest rate started sliding down to 9 per cent. I will admit that I am not too unhappy with the 10 per cent rate today. It will be paid off in due course.
I ask the minister to give consideration to the fact that the Federal Business Development Bank lends money at certain interest rates. I brought this matter up a few weeks ago. Up until three weeks ago, the bank lent money at the very high rate of 19 per cent. Even with the sliding interest rates of today, as the minister knows, the interest rate in the Federal Business Development Bank is 1744 per cent. Needless to say, we hope that will be amended within the next week or so. That is pretty tough, but the hardest part of it all is that the borrower is locked in for five years. With the high interest rates, the mortgages on homes and so on, banks are providing one-year mortgages in the hope that the interest rates would
Federal Business Development Bank Act go down. They have gone down, but it would seem that some of the FBDB new applications and renewals were renewed at 19 per cent a month or two ago. I can imagine what those business people are saying today. They are wringing their hands and are probably saying things not only under their breath. The loans are at 19 per cent and they cannot change this for four or five years, or whatever the case may be.
It would seem to me that the Federal Business Development Bank could operate like the chartered banks and say, "All right, we know it is a very bad time; we will give you a one-year mortgage which will be adjusted when we think things will work out a little better". Again I want to bring that to the attention of the minister.
I am also well aware that the rates of the Federal Business Development Bank are not competitive. From time to time 1 have told, and I still think of it as the IDB as it is easier to say, the Federal Business Development Bank that their rates are higher than one can get from a trust company, if one wanted the money for a building, or to put up a building, or from a chartered bank. I have advised people that they had better look into every avenue to get the best rate.
Again this comes down to the matter of the lender of last resort. Often many of the applicants do not qualify for loans from chartered banks or other institutions. As a last resort they go to the Federal Business Development Bank. Mention has been made about the higher loss ratio in respect of that government agency. 1 still suggest, as some others have done, the government should be there to try to help these small businesses gel on their feet and remain on their feet. I am also delighted, Mr. Speaker, and Mr. Minister, that this can even be enlarged, so that rather than for bricks, mortar and machinery the bank will lend for working capital.
There are a great many small businesses today which, because of the serious financial situation and general outlook, are finding it pretty difficult to keep afloat. If they have an existing loan and they are able to get some extra money to be used for working capital, and they approach the bank on that basis with some assets, I would hope the bank would consider them in a most sympathetic manner. This is most important.
One of the other things I want to comment on is the facilities which the bank provides; counselling to businessmen and offering them various types of services. This is very excellent. Seminars are held, as mentioned by the previous speaker, to which businessmen can go and lay their troubles on the table, and the bank can send someone down, very knowledgeable, in a particular type of business, to assist them in making more profits, and assist them if they are in financial difficulty so they can remain solvent. I would hope that if these businesses have viable objectives and plans, the bank would then step in and lend them this money.
I know that Bill C-20 is to be pul through, so I will sit down and let the minister speak, as I am sure he would like to make a few comments to wrap it up.

May 23, 1980
Federal Business Development Bank Act

The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and other departments should imitate the efforts made by the bank these last few years to bring its services to its customers on the customers' own grounds. I would like to join with my colleagues in this House in addressing my sincere congratulations to the president of the bank for having made the most of this policy.

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF "O CANADA" AS NATIONAL ANTHEM
speechtext:
That Bill C-220, respecting the national anthem of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to use all of my allotted time this afternoon. The intent of my private member's bill is well known to the hon. members of this House, and it is not my intention to elucidate the obvious. Mine is a measure which has no partisan overtones. Bill C-220 clearly is a measure which seeks to formalize in legislation a generally accepted and important element of our heritage and our nationhood.
A national anthem, like a national flag, is an important external symbol of nationhood. Yet here we are after 113 years of confederation without an official national anthem. I do not seek personal identification with this measure. 1 do not introduce it for personal or selfish gain. Instead, I see myself as a lowly backbencher, as a catalyst representing the aspirations and ambitions of my colleagues in this chamber and my millions of fellow-Canadians across this great land.
I began my research in the Thirty-first Parliament fully intending to introduce my private member's bill at that time. It was not until this Thirty-second Parliament that I had an opportunity to raise the matter in this House. I want to thank the government for allowing me the opportunity to place Bill C-220 before this House. I understand from Beauchesne's that when bills sponsored by members are called, that they are allowed to stand only at the request of the government and not at the request of the sponsor. I am indeed grateful to the government for causing this private bill to see the light of day.
The chronology of events which culminates here this hour has occurred with sudden swiftness. The sudden swiftness and the apparent unanimity reinforce my belief that a backbencher is not redundant in Parliament and even the lowliest private member has a special niche in the universe which unfolds. In my maiden speech of May 12, I announced my intentions regarding an official national anthem by way of Bill C-220.
On May 15 the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis), seconded by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard), attempted to have passed under Standing Order 43 a motion which officially recognizes "O Canada" as the national anthem and "God Save the Queen" as the royal anthem. The motion did not receive the required unanimous consent.
The following day another motion under Standing Order 43 introduced by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), on my behalf, failed to receive the necessary consent. In Hansard of May 16 at page 1145, after this Standing Order was introduced, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is reported as saying:
No. What are the words?
National Anthem
I would just like to say that the words are those which have been accepted in both English and French by every school child and every citizen of Canada. They are the words which everybody knows. On May 21 a motion under Standing Order 43 by the member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) calling on the government to introduce legislation as soon as possible with a view to designating "O Canada" as the national anthem did receive the unanimous consent of the House.
This brings us to 4 p.m., Friday, May 23, 1980, and Bill C-220, a private member's bill, which could readily be adopted as a government measure, should the government concur. I am approaching the end of my remarks. I hope to be the only speaker from my party. It is obvious from the motion under Standing Order 43 by the hon. member for Joliette that my party supports the intent of my bill. For that reason I believe members of my party have agreed to stand down in this debate and allow me to be the sole spokesman.
"O Canada" has its roots in the formation and development of this great nation. Its genesis goes back to the year 1880 when it was suggested that a competition be held for the composition of a national anthem. Some of the principals involved in the evolution of "O Canada" were Mr. Justice Routhier; the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, Dr. Theodore Robitaille; the famous French Canadian composer, Calixa Lavallee; and music editor Arthur Lavigne. It has its prime roots in French Canada.
It was not until the turn of the century in 1908 that an English version composed by Robert Stanley Weir gradually came into use. In 1924 the Association of Canadian Clubs endorsed Weir's version as a suitable anthem to be sung at all Canadian Club meetings. At the same time the Weir version was printed in many school readers in several provinces and was given official recognition by the federal and provincial governments on many important occasions.
The Weir version was used to mark the fiftieth anniversary of confederation on July 1, 1917. As stated previously, the words proposed are those which are in common usage in both English and French. In 1948, by order in council, it became the anthem of Canada's Armed Forces and they were required to salute it. Similarly, the Department of External Affairs provided that "O Canada" be accorded the recognition of the national anthem of Canada. In 1967 the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons recommended that the government be authorized to adopt the music of "O Canada", as composed by Calixa Lavallee, as the music for the national anthem.
The government of the day has, on four separate occasions in two Parliaments, introduced bills to adopt "O Canada" as the national anthem. None of these bills went beyond first reading stage. In 1978 the member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) introduced Bill C-438 respecting the national anthem. We have an opportunity this afternoon to pass into law a measure which has, through 100 years of usage, become a fact of life.
It is not my intention nor my desire to throttle or stifle free speech or debate. But the fact remains that my measure may

May 23, 1980
National Anthem
easily be talked out and disappear completely. 1 urge hon. members to consider it in the national interest, not as partisans but as patriots. Give it your support. In Beauchesne, section 217, at page 74 we find the following:
If it is evident that no member claims the right of speaking, the Speaker proceeds to put the question by reading the main motion ... He then takes the sense of the members of the last of these by saying: "Those who are in favour of the motion ... will say 'yea'.
Mr. Speaker, and hon. members, say yea for "O Canada", say yea for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF "O CANADA" AS NATIONAL ANTHEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate this afternoon. 1 should advise the hon. member that the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) will be here later in the debate to comment on this bill. I think from the outset that we should say that there probably will not be a disposition to talk this bill out, as is often the practice. But I cannot guarantee that, because I have not talked with the minister this afternoon. The minister is very glad to have an opportunity to participate in the debate and is very happy that the hon. member has come forward today.
Since we do have a few minutes before the minister comes- and I understand that other members wish to speak-I would like to say a few words. This past week has been a very traumatic one for Canada. It has been one where one particular region, the province of Quebec, voted by a significant margin to stay within Canada. I am sure that all members of the House applaud that vote. The feeling around this House this week is a feeling which I have never experienced in my years in this House of Commons.
There seems to be good will on all sides and a disposition on matters of national unity and the constitution to work together. That is not to say that all parties will agree on every particular item that will be discussed in the forthcoming constitutional debates, but as I said last night in a debate which was very graciously provided for us by the New Democratic Party on their opposition day, this has been a difficult time for us, and we now must come together as politicians from all sides of this House to deal with the future of our country and the future structures in our country on an almost non-partisan basis. I hope that in the speeches which ensue this afternoon members will follow in that vein.
I would like to talk about symbols. "O Canada" has been a symbol in this country for many years. It has been a symbol, as the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) suggested, of the history of Canada. It was written by a Canadian of French-speaking origin many years ago, and has had wide usage within the country. It is unofficially Canada's national anthem. It is a symbol. I can remember as a young boy of ten years old being in the immigration office in London when our family applied to come to this country-at the time Canada was trying to entice immigrants-seeing a film by the Canadian government which depicted the different regions of the country. I remember at the end of that film, Mr. Speaker, the closing credits came on with the then flag of Canada, the Red
Ensign, and the music of "O Canada" sung by an armed forces chorus. I had never heard the song before and, even as a ten-year-old, I was quite moved. It had an appeal for me. Little did I know that some 23 years later, or less, I would be a member of this House of Commons and speaking on the very future of that symbolic song.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I would welcome, as I am sure every member of the House would, the adoption of "O Canada" as the official anthem of this country.
There are some other symbols I wish to talk about, however, as they have equal meaning. One is a symbol for many people of British origin, and that is the anthem "God Save the Queen". I think it is fair to say that not all members of the chamber have the same attachment to that anthem. As one who grew up in Great Britain I have a particular attachment to the royal anthem. I do not think that if we pass this bill, or if the government brings in a bill-as I understand is likely- to make "O Canada" the official anthem and if it does become the official anthem, that that would in any way diminish the royal anthem which is played on all suitable occasions. I would hope that in accepting the symbol of "O Canada" we would not forget that part of our heritage which is reflected in the British fact and the royal anthem.
We also have the flag as a symbol. Some 16 years ago this House was torn apart in the debate over the flag. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was here then, perhaps also the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and, of course, yourself Mr. Speaker. You will remember that in 1964 there was an emotional tearing apart of the House on the adoption of the flag, and I think for good reason. The Red Ensign had great historical significance for Canada. It was a flag under which Canadians fought in the Boer War, the First World War, and the Second World War. It had great significance for most Canadians-so much so that the province of Ontario has seen fit to retain it as the provincial flag.
In those 16 years the flag we now have, the single red maple leaf, has become the living symbol of Canadian unity. I remember thumbing my way through Europe in 1967, as I am sure many other hon. members have done. I remember the kind of rapport that was struck up between my friend and I and the people in various countries we visited, and how the Canadian maple leaf was recognized as the symbol of Canada. That was only three years after it had been adopted by this House and the wounds still had not healed.
There was great pride-I would not say jingoistic pride, although I suppose there is competition between Canadians and our friends to the south-in having the Canadian maple leaf on our packs and saying to the Americans we met that we were a separate country from them although we might speak the same language with a similar accent. We have a different country and a sort of different heritage, some of it common to that of the United States, but there is a distinctive difference in this country which is enhanced by the fact of two official languages and the many cultures that have decided to call
May 23, 1980

Canada home. 1 wanted to mention a couple of those symbols, Mr. Speaker. In the previous opportunities 1 have had to speak I have dealt with the constitutional question and not participated in some of the emotional aspects of the unity debate that we saw this week.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I am very grateful that the hon. member has seen fit to persevere with his bill and bring it forward again. I think it was fitting that it be called today. Hon. members wanted him to proceed with it and that is why the other bills were stood.
1 wish to reiterate my personal support and, 1 am sure, that of every member in the House. The Secretary of State will be here shortly to make some significant comment on the question of national unity and the symbolism implied and inherent in Bill C-220 which will make "O Canada" our official anthem.

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF "O CANADA" AS NATIONAL ANTHEM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF "O CANADA" AS NATIONAL ANTHEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful and proud as a Canadian to be allowed to speak on this particular issue. Legislation to make "O Canada" our official national anthem is long overdue-I should even like to suggest it is exactly 100 years overdue. It was back in 1880 that Mr. Justice Routhier penned the original French words in 1880, and later that same year Mr. Calixa Lavallee put this poem to music. This anthem was found to be very popular among French Canadians, so much so that it supplanted other French Canadian patriotic songs in existence at that time.
We are aware, of course, that there are many English versions of "O Canada" which have been put to Lavallee's original musical score. The most generally accepted English version, however, was that composed in 1908 by Robert Stanley Weir. The English version has undoubtedly met with the same popularity as the French version.
I feel we must press to officially declare "O Canada" as our national anthem. There is no doubt in my mind that the euphoria created in this House due to the rather welcome outcome of the Quebec referendum was one of the major catalysts behind the unanimous acceptance of a motion on Wednesday, May 21, requesting that "O Canada" be adopted as our national anthem. I think it is appropriate that positive action be taken, and 1 hope that members of the House will consider doing so this afternoon.
National symbols such as flags, anthems, and emblems play a very important role in our life. They represent and project an image of our land, they provide us with a link to our heritage, and in this manner give us a feeling of continuity and serve to evoke in each of us a more clear conceptualization of our identity as Canadians.
I also feel that national symbols draw us closer to our fellow Canadians in the realization that we all share many things in common. This was part of Robert Stanley Weir's reason for writing English words to Lavallee's tune. He said:
In 1908 it occurred to me that there was an opportunity, by the medium of music, to supply English-speaking Canada with English words which could be sung to the same melody that our French Canadian fellow countrymen were
National Anthem
making use of. With one national song as to music, what mattered if the words differed as regards language.
Let us all, in unison, join with one heart and mind in support of this motion.
In examining the bill before us, I invite all hon. members of the House to take a look in four directions with me.
First of all, this bill causes me to look back. I look back to the time of the birth of our nation. I speak of the crisis of confederation. More precisely, I look at the spirit of confederation. One morning, in designating and identifying what Canada would be, Sir Leonard Tilley turned to psalm 72, verse 8. He shared with his colleagues the following words from the psalmist David "And his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, from the river even to the ends of the earth." "From sea to sea" is the origin of the legend on the Canadian coat of arms.
In the last two decades our self-identity has been enhanced by two other symbols of our confederation. Under Prime Minister Diefenbaker we adopted a Canadian Bill of Rights. While Lester B. Pearson was our prime minister we adopted a new Canadian flag. More recently on May 20, Quebeckers forced us to examine ourselves again and realize afresh that we are a nation. A most fitting national memorial to the occasion of the referendum would be to adopt "O Canada" as our national anthem recognizing that originally a French Canadian had written the anthem for us.

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF "O CANADA" AS NATIONAL ANTHEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) for his sentiments in bringing before this House the bill proposing that "O Canada" be declared Canada's national anthem.
I do not wish to be labelled as an opportunist who is trying to talk out this bill, but I think it is too good an opportunity for a person like myself who considers himself to be a patriot to say something about this great and wonderful country of ours.
When I came into this House I questioned the fact that I might not have had enough experience nor had particular expertise as a lawyer, or whatever else is required, to be a good parliamentarian, but I do feel that I have one thing that all of us have, and that is I have experience of living in the greatest country of the world, and that makes me an expert as far as 1 am concerned on this subject of how one can love this country.
My friend on these benches mentioned something about the fact that so many of our patriots leave this great country and go south of the border. There is an old saying in this country, "If you can't lick 'em, join 'em." So what I did was to join with an American and now she is living in this country with me and enjoying the great fruits of our country. I am not so sure what happens to my children. My father was of German extraction. My mother's family are Scottish; I married an American of Norwegian extraction, so what that makes my children, I am not so sure. But I know one thing, it does make them citizens of the greatest country in the world.
I do not know whether many of you have been in that area of Ontario which has Fort St. Marie Among the Hurons, which is in the Midland area. If you have never been there and you want to experience something worth while, you should visit the fort. It has been completely reconstructed. At first you are shown a movie of the trials and tribulations of the French and the Hurons and all of the things they went through to try to establish themselves in Canada. As hon. members probably know, in order that the enemy not take over the fort, as the enemy approached the Hurons and the missionaries burned the fort to the ground so that it could not fall into enemy hands. At the back of the theatre there are some doors which rise and, just as the film concludes, the last picture depicts the whole fort burning. As the doors rise, the audience, on departure, walk through the flames, which are filmed on the doors. It is a most exciting and moving experience.
Recently I took some visitors from Britain to see the movie and the fort. They told me, and it may sound rather provincial on my part, that for the first time they really understood the French attitude in Canada because this whole story was mainly about the French and the Indians. It was a very moving experience.
I talked about my American experience, and the thing that really impressed me there was the fact that in the city of Minneapolis they have such names as Minnie-ha-ha, Minnetonka, and Scottish names like MacPhail. When you drive down the street you may see a sign which points to a place called Douglas. Then you have French names like LeSoeur, LaSalle, indicating that the roots that were established by the early explorers of this country, the fur traders and other people, have extended right across the continent. I am sure that is why we have this tremendous common bond with our neighbours to the south. We are more alike than we are different, and much of this is due to the kind of heritage that we all have.
I remember when I was reasonably young at the beginning of the Second World War. Some of my relatives said, "Son, just make sure you keep your patriotism in the sole of your shoe." They had been through a war and had seen what happened. They were telling me, "Look, don't get involved in this war," but my patriotism came to the fore. I had no difficulty in volunteering to serve my country, this great country of Canada. After having been in North Africa, Sicily,
May 23, 1980

Italy and northwest Europe, England and Scotland, how proud I was all the time 1 was in these countries to be a Canadian.
1 am going to talk a little bit on how this national anthem came about. It gives me an opportunity to mention my riding in this respect. This national anthem "O Canada" came about because of a contest to try to have a national anthem for a particular purpose some 100 years ago. It is interesting that we have in my constituency the Guelph Spring Festival which each year sponsors a contest to try to encourage young Canadian musicians to go on with their work and become successful musicians.
There has been no doubt for many years that when a national anthem is declared in this country, it will be "O Canada". Both tradition and custom vest it with this distinction, although it never has been acknowledged as such by an act of Parliament or by proclamation. Over the years a solidarity of sentiment has developed in the hearts of the preponderance of Canadians that "O Canada" is our national anthem. As a matter of fact we are not dealing with a consensus that we ought to have a national anthem, rather, we are dealing with a solidarity of sentiment that we already have a national anthem, "O Canada." This sentiment is one that should have a very special meaning for us at this very specific and happy time, when our compatriots in Quebec have affirmed their faith in a united Canada.
"O Canada" is the artistic creation of three men; of Adolphe Basile Routhier, who wrote the French words, of Calixa Lavallee who wrote the music for Routhier's words, and of Robert Stanley Weir whose English lyrics, written for Laval-lee's music, is the one among many such attempts around which a solid public sentiment has grown.
I would like to present a brief history of "O Canada". Its origins, I submit, are quite pertinent to our deliberations and I feel that an account of them should be on the public record. The subject is of direct, even personal, interest to Canadians all across the country. Yet the details of the story of "O Canada," while in no way obscure or complex, are not widely known.
Shortly after confederation in 1880, Quebec City was preparing for a great gathering, the first national French Canadian convention. This was to be a great public occasion. The program included a patriotic banquet attended by the Governor General of the day, the Marquis of Lome, and his wife, Princess Louise. There was also to be a high mass celebrated in the open air by the Archbishop of Quebec.
The committee arranging the congress had plans for commissioning a patriotic song and there was a scheme for holding an open competition. The winning entry would have its first public performance June 24, 1880, the feast of Saint-Jean-Baptiste, for the dates of the convention had been set to include this most important French holiday.
We can all imagine the mountain of details that must have preoccupied the organizational committee. Not only was the occasion to involve the highest leaders of state and church, but many French-speaking visitors were expected from both near
National Anthem
and far. We can understand, also, how time slipped by until the group responsible for finding a patriotic song realized that it was too late to launch such a competition. Indeed, that is what appears to have happened.
The next turn of events may inspire gratitude for the foresight of the Fathers of Confederation in providing for the post of Lieutenant Governor. Or perhaps our thanks should be for the good fortune that placed a man on the scene who must have combined a good deal of perception with inventive initiative.
This man was Theodore Robitaille, Quebec's Lieutenant Governor at the time. He was a person well acquainted with events and developments in the Quebec capital. When he learned of the committee's decision to drop plans for developing a national song, he simply took matters into his own hands.
His first move was to approach a judge of the Superior Court of Quebec, Adolphe Basile Routhier, who was well known as an orator and man of letters. Would the judge produce a suitable poem? The judge would; and the judge did. Next the Lieutenant Governor called on Calixa Lavallee.
Now, almost a hundred years later, it is almost impossible to get a satisfactory assessment of Judge Routhier's status in the literary world of his day. This kind of assessment is somewhat easier in the case of Lavallee. He was then the leading musical figure in Canada. He had studied in Europe as well as in Canada and the United States. He had a reputation that was both solid and international.
In retrospect, Lieutenant-Governor Robitaille's commission to Lavallee-a commission to compose the air for a patriotic song-came at a most inauspicious time in the maestro's career. Only shortly before, Lavallee had composed, produced and conducted a musical tour de force in honour of the Governor General and Princess Louise. Although the event seems to have been a success in every other way, it turned out to be a financial disaster for Lavallee.
Calixa Lavallee had read the writing on the wall. To remain in Canada would mean a future of routine teaching and playing. Indeed, at the time of Robitaille's commission, he was on the point of making a decision that too many talented Canadians have had to make since; that decision was to leave Canada for broader horizons and, in Lavallee's case as in so many others, that meant moving to the United States.
But to return to the events of 1880, Lavallee seems to have accepted the assignment with real enthusiasm; to compose a setting for Judge Routhier's poem. And quickly.
Nor did Calixa Lavallee waste any time. Apparently only a week or so went by before he had the music sketched out on paper. He tried the melody out on some of his friends. They agreed. It was the real thing. So Lavallee ran off to have the music copied and placed in the hands of Theodore Robitaille.
As things turned out, the work of Routhier and Lavallee was not performed exactly as had been planned originally, that is, during the outdoor mass on Saint-Jean-Baptiste day. Its debut

May 23, 1980
National Anthem
came the next day at the patriotic banquet attended by the Governor General and by Theodore Robitaille, no doubt in his role as Lieutenant Governor. The immediate response was enthusiastic. Those in attendance applauded. "The new national air is striking and was well received", reported the Quebec Morning Chronicle. Arthur Lavigne, a figure on the Quebec musical scene, rushed sheet music of "O Canada" into print.
And then, nothing. For almost 20 years "O Canada" was seldom heard. Calixa Lavallee died in Boston in 1891 with no inkling of the place his work was to take in his native land. Indeed, the piece was not even listed in the summary of his accomplishments set out in his obituary. And the writer of a biography of Sir Adolphe Routhier which came out in 1898 did not consider "O Canada" significant enough even to be mentioned.
But the words of Judge Routhier and the music of Calixa Lavallee were not forgotten. Their emergence from obscurity was described in a column in Le Devoir on November 6, 1915, by Arthur Letondal, as follows:
It had yet to capture the public imagination, and this was to take some time. One cannot dictate to a people what its patriotic songs should be any more than one can impose a new work on the language. It takes time and a special combination of circumstances to awaken national sentiment and win its support. And 20 years were to pass before the song again attracted attention. What finally prompted this we cannot say but we do know that around the year 1900, by some sort of mysterious understanding, certain groups . . . began to campaign in favour of what we then called "l.avallee's Anthem". Our concerts and festivals all concluded with the song and enthusiasm for it grew daily. This was the beginning. Editions soon appeared with English lyrics spreading it across the country. It has now been definitely adopted throughout the nation and its popularity is uncontesled.
What we might call the first formal or official exposure of "O Canada" in a purely English-speaking event seems to have occurred when it was played during a tattoo at the military camp at N iagara in 1900. The next year, in 1901, "O Canada" was one of the airs played by massed bands as the Duke of Cornwall, who was to become King George V, reviewed troops who had assembled in Toronto from all over Ontario.
Then, five years later, the firm of Whaley, Royce and Company in Toronto published the music with Sir Adolphe Routhier's original French words and an English version by a Toronto physician, Dr. Thomas Bedford Richardson.
During those early years of this century almost a whole catalogue of English lyrics was proposed to be sung with Lavallee's music. The height of this flurry of poetic activity was related to the 1908 celebration of the three-hundredth anniversary of the founding of Quebec.

I would like to add that during this campaign, "O Canada" became a true rallying point, much like our flag, the single red maple leaf, for everyone who expressed their faith in the Canadian federation.

At this time, I should like to quote to the House the motion just mentioned by the hon. member, the motion passed on May 21, and explain why it is imperative that we proceed as indicated in the motion, instead of by way of the bill which comes to us, without warning, this afternoon. I quote the motion passed on May 21:
That this House unanimously call on the government to introduce legislation as soon as possible with a view to designating "O Canada" as the national anthem of the country.
By supporting that motion, all parties in the House expressed the wish that the government introduce legislation as soon as possible to make "O Canada" the official anthem of the country. Since the government is getting ready to act to that effect, and implement the motion the House passed unanimously, well, Mr. Speaker, 1 would much rather vote for a government bill instead of making a decision in this House, this afternoon, with a handful of well-intentioned hon. members, and give that decision which I consider important all the decorum it deserves.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to remind this House that it was as a result of a motion under Standing Order 43 that the Canadian flag was introduced into this House and given the place it occupies on your right; and also that last year, in this House, an hon. member moved, during private members' hour, that Dominion Day be changed to Canada Day.
Well, that hon. members in a spirit of magnanimity and with good intentions should have let such a bill be referred to a committee, returned to the House and then that such a bill should be talked out by some members on third reading, then, Mr. Speaker, if we want to adopt the national anthem 1 have been waiting for for a very long time, I would like that national anthem to enter by the front door, not the back door. After the decision we took to keep Quebec in confederation, at a time when the people of Quebec decided to go with Canada in terms of their future, I think they deserve to have that decision followed up by an official decision that will give us once and for all the national anthem we have been wanting for several years.
There is no doubt that passing this bill would be just as valuable and as important a decision as if we waited for the government's, but 1 think the national anthem of my country should be adopted in a bill that could perhaps include an amendment so the name "Dominion Day" would become "Canada Day". That is one thing 1 hope and I recommend greatly to the government and the responsible minister.
My insistence this afternoon is not to refuse the adoption of the national anthem, my insistence and my participation in this debate is to recognize the merit of that anthem that has been sung for years by generations of Canadians officially or unofficially, that is being sung to the glory of Canada by a Canadian, Roger Doucet, who made it known across the world
National Anthem
and to whom I want to pay tribute today, a national anthem that is already recognized internationally and which deserves to come in this Parliament through the front door. Not only do we owe it legally that official status but we must also ensure that "O Canada" is used more from coast to coast in this country. We will be able to do that only if we can build a country of which all Canadians can be proud, a country whose constitution reflects the geographic reality and the democratic ideal that is ours. Our national anthem must become a symbol of the modern Canada we all aspire to, the brotherly Canada we should build together to meet the fundamental aspirations of its citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I am in total agreement with the reasons that prompted the hon. member for Simcoe South to introduce his motion. 1 support the principle and the aim of his proposal, to give us a national anthem, but 1 would much rather have that important gesture that is basic to our country's future, a gesture of Canadian unity, proceed within the standards and norms of the great honours that can often be confessed at the right time by this House, and I would invite the government to indicate the time-frame, hopefully short, within which they propose to act on the resolution that called unanimously for the official designation of the national anthem, and hopefully change the name "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day".
